claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a metastable, single-phase solid solution with negligible intermetallic precipitation.
Controlled thermal aging can drive microstructural or phase evolution in the alloy.
Localized thermal activation during service or aging promotes Mg partitioning out of the metastable solid solution.
Mg partitioning nucleates Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates nucleate primarily at grain boundaries.
Diffusion in the alloy is intrinsically sluggish because of its high-configurational-entropy state.
Transformation kinetics determine whether Mg-rich precipitates remain fine and coherent or become coarse and incoherent.
A fine, coherent dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallics supports formation of a continuous, adherent protective oxide scale.
A fine, coherent dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallics maintains or enhances corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
A fine, coherent dispersion of Mg-rich intermetallics maintains or enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Coarse, incoherent intermetallics disrupt the continuity of protective oxide layers.
Coarse intermetallic formation or substantial coarsening degrades corrosion resistance.
Coarse intermetallic formation or substantial coarsening degrades high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The as-cast or as-processed metastable state initially has high corrosion and oxidation resistance.
Transformation kinetics become significant under corrosive or oxidative service conditions at approximately 600–900 °C.
The critical temperature and duration separating beneficial fine precipitation from deleterious coarsening are not yet constrained.
The effect of Mg on the composition of the protective oxide remains to be quantitatively established.
